answer: Judgment: partly value-accretive, but not unequivocally so. B&PB added revenue, underlying profit and cash earnings, while the full-year credit-charge rate edged down. However, earnings lagged lending growth, annual NIM compressed under competitive pressure, and cash returns on assets declined. Growth therefore created absolute value, but diluted unit economics; the stronger second half suggests stabilisation rather than proof that pricing has fully recovered. Business lending rose 7.3% to $166.3bn, housing 5.8% to $109.3bn and GLAs 6.8% to $279.5bn. Net operating income increased 2.1% to $8,531m; underlying profit and cash earnings each grew 1.6%, to $5,299m and $3,330m. NIM fell 8 bps to 3.01%; cash earnings/average assets fell 5 bps to 1.25%, while cash earnings/average RWA fell 1 bp to 2.18%. NAB attributes the margin decline to competitive pressures in both lending books and higher deposit costs, although NIM improved from 3.01% in 1H25 to 3.02% in 2H25. FY25 CIC was $529m versus $523m and CIC/GLAs improved 1 bp to 0.19%, but NPEs rose from $5,580m/2.12% to $7,079m/2.54%, while 2H CIC rose to $292m/0.21% from $237m/0.18%. Lending growth was broad across Agri, Health, CRE and Other. In contrast, NAB says the September-versus-March B&PB default-but-not-impaired deterioration mainly reflected single names; the agriculture NPL uplift was mainly two large, well-secured customers. Overall: positive dollar accretion, but weaker unit returns and emerging asset-quality pressure prevent a clean quality-growth verdict.

limitations: NAB does not disclose B&PB new-business spreads, sector-level margins, cohort loss performance, economic profit, or a divisional ROE/hurdle-rate comparison.
The disclosure does not quantify how much of the full-year NPE increase was single-name driven; the explicit attribution covers September 2025 versus March 2025.
The agriculture single-name disclosure is at the Australian industry level, not explicitly limited to B&PB.

Customer lending and deposit portfolios were transferred between Personal Banking and B&PB during FY25; comparatives were restated, but the disclosed series still cannot reveal organic customer-level growth.
Cash earnings is a non-IFRS performance measure, so it does not by itself establish economic value creation.
